summary: Generalizes the use of a packet's TTL (IPv4) or Hop Limit (IPv6) to protect protocols from CPU-utilization attacks. It suits protocols such as BGP, MSDP and LDP, especially between directly connected peers. It is experimental and has been replaced by RFC 5082.

eli5.summary: If you only talk to your next-door neighbor, a shout from far away is suspicious. This trick checks a packet's travel counter to ignore messages that came from too far away. RFC 5082 replaced it.

questions: how to protect routers from remote attacks using ttl
subtitle: Using the packet hop count to prevent attacks on routing protocols from distant sources.

tldr.problem: Routing protocols like BGP run on routers' control planes and are vulnerable to CPU-overload attacks from any source on the Internet. Cryptographic protection is expensive; however, most protocol peerings are between directly connected routers, and TTL spoofing from a distance is nearly impossible.
tldr.mechanism: Set outbound packets for protocol sessions to maximum TTL (255). For each configured peer, reject inbound protocol packets that do not have the expected TTL (255 for direct peers, 255 minus the expected hop count for multi-hop peers). This filters out most distant attacks with no cryptographic overhead.
tldr.outcome: A simple, widely deployable defense against CPU-based DDoS attacks on infrastructure protocols, effective for directly connected peers. GTSM is experimental and was superseded by RFC 5082.

today: RFC 3682 is experimental and has been superseded by RFC 5082, which provides a more refined specification and additional deployment guidance for GTSM. However, GTSM protection is widely deployed in production networks as a first-line defense against infrastructure attacks.

sections.title: The Attack and the Defense
sections.content:
GTSM (Generalized TTL Security Mechanism) protects a router's control plane from CPU-overload attacks by using the TTL (Time to Live) field in the IP header. The mechanism is based on a simple observation: the vast majority of protocol peerings between routers are between directly connected neighbors. When two routers are directly connected, a legitimate protocol packet must have a TTL of 255 (the maximum). A packet claiming to be from an adjacent peer but with a TTL below 255 must have originated from farther away, either spoofed or legitimately sent from another router but misdirected.

By checking the TTL of inbound protocol packets and rejecting those that do not match the expected value, a router can filter out most attacks from distant sources before they reach the CPU. This is particularly effective for defense against CPU-utilization based attacks, where an attacker floods a protocol peer with traffic designed to consume processing resources.

The mechanism is named "generalized" because while it originated as a technique for BGP, it applies equally well to other protocols like MSDP (Multicast Source Discovery Protocol), LDP (Label Distribution Protocol), and BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection).
sections.eli5: A shout from far away takes a long time to arrive, so each router who passes it along reduces a special counter (the TTL). Your neighbor cannot have that counter reduced much. If you get a message from someone claiming to be your neighbor but the counter is almost zero, they are lying.

sections.title: Assumptions and Limitations
sections.content:
GTSM rests on four key assumptions. First, most protocol peerings are between adjacent routers. Second, service providers typically ingress-filter (deny) packets with the provider's own loopback addresses as the source, preventing some classes of spoofed traffic. Third, GTSM is optional and configured per peer, allowing incremental deployment. Fourth, the router can classify traffic destined for the routing processor into control and non-control queues.

GTSM is most effective against directly connected peers and assumes no compromise of adjacent routers in the path. For multi-hop peerings (where protocol peers are not directly adjacent), GTSM provides weaker protection: an attacker could theoretically launch an attack by compromising a router in the path. The RFC assumes such attacks would cause worse problems than just forged protocol packets.

GTSM cannot protect protocols that use flooding mechanisms (like multicast) and is not automatically negotiated between peers. Administrators must manually configure GTSM on both sides of a peering relationship.
sections.eli5: This trick works best when routers are right next to each other. It assumes bad guys cannot hijack the routers in between, and that you turned on the setting yourself when both routers are ready.

sections.title: How GTSM Works
sections.content:
When GTSM is enabled for a peer, the router follows this procedure. For direct peers, it sets the outbound TTL for all protocol packets to 255. On the receive path, it configures an Access Control List (ACL) to allow protocol packets to reach the route processor only if they have the expected source address, destination address, and TTL tuple.

For a directly connected peer, the expected TTL is 255. For a multi-hop peer, the expected TTL is 255 minus the configured acceptable hop range, providing robustness to small topology changes. Any packet that does not match the expected TTL is not processed. Instead, it is placed in a low-priority queue and silently discarded or logged. No ICMP message is generated in response.

When GTSM is not enabled, normal protocol behavior is followed without any TTL checking.
sections.eli5: Send out your messages with the counter set to 255. Check incoming messages for a counter of 255 (for neighbors) or the right lower number (for farther peers). Ignore anything that does not match.

sections.title: Edge Cases and Protections
sections.content:
GTSM has important limitations in certain scenarios. When a protocol packet is tunneled (such as IP-in-IP or GRE), the tunnel endpoint can set the inner TTL to any value, potentially allowing an attacker to craft a tunneled packet with the expected TTL. MPLS tunneling presents a similar issue: the TTL field handling in MPLS can result in a maximum egress TTL of 254, not 255, making direct TTL checking impossible for MPLS-encapsulated packets.

For intra-domain protocol peers (such as iBGP speakers within a single AS), GTSM is often not used. Instead, the RFC recommends filtering at the network edge to reject any packets with the loopback addresses used for intra-domain peering as the source, combined with MD5-based BGP session authentication for stronger protection.

Multi-hop protocol sessions receive only optional GTSM support. The RFC acknowledges that full protection of multi-hop sessions requires cryptographic machinery such as Secure BGP (S-BGP) rather than relying solely on TTL checks.
sections.eli5: Tunnels can mess things up because they reset the counter. Very important internal routers should use other locks (like passwords). Far-away peers should use real encryption instead of just counting hops.

sections.title: What GTSM Protects and Does Not Protect
sections.content:
GTSM provides simple protection for single-hop protocol sessions when neither peer is compromised. It does not provide authentication, encryption, or replay protection. It does not protect against attacks originating from a compromised peer or compromised intermediate router. Its primary value is raising the bar against opportunistic CPU-overload attacks.

The RFC emphasizes that TTL spoofing from non-adjacent locations is considered nearly impossible under normal router operation (where each router decrements TTL by one). However, tunneling mechanisms create exceptions where the inner packet TTL can be set to arbitrary values. In those cases, additional controls at the tunnel endpoints are needed.

GTSM works alongside other security mechanisms. It does not replace cryptographic authentication and should be used as part of a defense-in-depth strategy. For protocols like BGP, combining GTSM (for directly connected external peers) with MD5-based session authentication (for internal iBGP peers) provides both simplicity and security.
sections.eli5: GTSM is a speed bump, not a fortress. It stops lazy attacks from far away, but it does not replace real security like passwords or encryption. Use both together.
